entry.title: I got tired of boring, "clean" SaaS UIs. So I built a Neo-Brutalist Web Utilities Platform from scratch. 🚀
entry.summary: Hey everyone, 👋 As developers, we constantly rely on random web utilities—JSON formatters, mock data generators, disposable emails. But let’s be real: most of these sites are either packed with annoying display ads, have a generic "clean corporate" UI that blinds you at 2 AM, or they put basic features behind a paywall. I wanted something different. I wanted a toolkit that felt like my terminal—dark, aggressive, fast, and straight to the point. No fluff, no ads, just raw utility. So, I built Zlvox. 🎨 The Vibe: Neo-Brutalist & Privacy-First High-contrast borders. Pitch-dark themes. Zero unnecessary animations. The goal was simple: you open the site, paste your data or get your tool running, and get out in seconds. Most importantly, it is privacy-first. Your data stays yours. 🛠️ What I've Built Inside Zlvox So Far: GhostMail: A totally free, fast disposable email generator. Perfect for testing auth flows without cluttering your personal inbox. Data Forge: A custom mock data generator. I got frustrated juggling between Faker.js and Mockaroo, so I built my own version that generates massive amounts of structured dummy data and SQL instantly. Plus a whole suite of client-side utilities (bug fixers, SQL generators, etc.) that run blazing fast. 💻 The Stack 🤔 I need your brutal feedback! I’d love for you to try it out: zlvox.com What do you think of the Neo-Brutalist design? Is it too raw, or exactly what you like? Try out Data Forge or GhostMail—what features are missing? What specific dev tool should I build and add to Zlvox next week? Drop your thoughts in the comments. I’ll be hanging around to answer any questions about the code, the design, or the struggle of building it solo! 🚀

entry.title: Exploring Deep and Wide Search: Insights from the DeepWideSearch Benchmark for LLM-based Agents
entry.summary: Introduction: Paper Summary: After extensive research, authors found out that even the best and most accomplished LLMs performed poorly on the benchmark, giving only a meagre success rate of 2.39 percent. In order to create this, the authors mainly suggested two conversion methods to generate more demanding task. 1 . Deep2Wide Conversion: In this method, already existing deep search benchmarks are taken which focus on reasoning and expands them by requiring agents to gather more information. Wide2Deep Conversion: In this one, wide search queries which consist of collecting information from various sources are modified by adding even more complex reasoning tasks, which would require the agent to perform multiple reasoning steps. Both of these combined make DeepWideSearch a rigorous test for modern search agents. Course Connections: The A* algorithm, which we have completed in our course consists of searching for the most optimal path. The major problem we face with that is that it is a single path search, compared to multi step reasoning and wide collection of data which is discussed in this paper in depth. This connection to my course, helps me understand in a better and more relevant way about the real life implications of these agents in high stakes environment such as business models etc. Personal Insights: Lack of reflection: Mainly agents don’t re-evaluate their mistakes and sometimes stop after hitting a problem, when they get stuck. This made me understand that even though large scale LLMs are very powerful, agent architecture has still their limitations. There is still a lot of work to be done in this regard, in order to make these systems work for real world handling complex tasks. entry.title: I analyzed 40 OpenClaw use cases — 92.5% don't need OpenClaw
entry.summary:
Why I Built This
I was looking at the awesome-openclaw-usecases repo — 40 real-world use cases for OpenClaw. It looked like a goldmine of automation ideas. But then I noticed something: almost none of them actually need OpenClaw. The "skills" are just API wrappers. The "memory system" is just file storage. The "sub-agents" are just parallel tasks. Every capability they depend on exists in any capable AI agent.
Classification Count %
Agent-agnostic (works anywhere) 20 50%
Partial (swap one tool) 17 42.5%
OpenClaw-dependent 3 7.5%
Only 3 out of 40 use cases genuinely require OpenClaw. The rest? They work with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or any agent with shell access + LLM reasoning. So I extracted the 37 agent-agnostic use cases. But dumping 37 guides into one skill file would burn ~30,000 tokens every invocation. That's wasteful. Instead, I used an Index Skill Pattern: SKILL.md is just a table of contents (~1,200 tokens) Each use case lives in its own file under usecases/
Only the selected file gets loaded on demand (~800 tokens) 93% context savings vs monolithic
not-need-claw/ ├── SKILL.md # Index skill (~1,200 tokens) └── usecases/ # 37 use cases (loaded on-demand) ├── second-brain.md ├── self-healing-home-server.md └── ... (35 more)
Social Media (4): Reddit/YouTube digest, X analysis, tech news aggregation Creative & Building (5): Podcast pipeline, game dev, content factory Infrastructure & DevOps (2): Self-healing server, n8n orchestration Productivity (18): Second brain, CRM, meeting notes, habit tracker Research & Learning (7): arXiv reader, RAG knowledge base, idea validator Finance (1): Polymarket autopilot npx skills add devjiro76/not-need-claw
GitHub: devjiro76/not-need-claw Looking for community contributions — if you have agent-agnostic use cases that work across platforms, PRs welcome. not-need-claw is open source. I'd love to hear your feedback!
